description: I am developing an interactive storytelling website for the NASA Space Apps Challenge project, Abandoned but Not Forgotten. Our project explores the stories of NASA equipment left on Moon and Mars, highlighting the mission challenges, discoveries, and lasting scientific engineering contributions.
summary:
**Abandoned, But Not Forgotten: Hardware stays. Knowledge inspires.**

What happens to spacecraft and equipment when their missions end? Some remain on the Moon or Mars, but the knowledge they helped us gain continues to be valuable.

This project is an interactive storytelling website about six NASA missions: Surveyor 3, Ranger 7, Apollo 15’s Lunar Roving Vehicle, InSight, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

Through mission cards, destination filters, and simple explanations, visitors can explore what these machines did, what scientists learned from them, and why their missions still matter. The goal is to help young space enthusiasts discover the stories behind space exploration and see how every mission can contribute to future discoveries.
details:
Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is an interactive website created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It explores six NASA missions connected to the Moon and Mars.

The website lets visitors explore individual missions, filter them by destination, and learn about the equipment, mission goals, discoveries, and challenges involved. It also includes questions to encourage curiosity and links to NASA resources for further learning.

I built the website using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and published it using GitHub Pages. I also created a Canva presentation and a short video to demonstrate the project.

I used AI tools to help with brainstorming, research interpretation, coding guidance, and troubleshooting. I made the project’s creative and development decisions and included NASA resources to help visitors explore the mission information further.

My aim is to make learning about space missions more interesting and accessible to young people, while showing that even when a mission ends, the knowledge gained can help shape future exploration.
